But No Man’s Sky isn’t presenting each player with a unique galaxy every time they fire it up. It’s using procedural generation to create the same sprawling galaxy with the same contents for every player to encounter, even though it’s so large that someone could play for the rest of their lives without stumbling upon a planet that another player has already explored. “In No Man’s Sky, everyone’s universe is built from the same seed,” says Cook. Specific numbers, or “seed values” are run through a series of algorithms – what Hello Games’ art director, Grant Duncan, calls “boxes of math” – to create a unique result. The blueprints of the entire universe have already been created using this technique, but the game only builds out a player’s immediate surroundings so as not to make your CPU melt down. Whenever you arrive on a planet, the game runs the preset seed values for that planet through the algorithm, thus summoning up that planet’s singular terrain, weather, flora, and fauna.

A couple of days before the game’s release, the developers announced that purchasers can download an update that will completely overhaul the game experience. Planets are moved around, some star systems are an order of magnitude larger, biomes and atmospheric systems are tweaked, and diversity of animal life is boosted. “We changed the rules of the universe generation algorithm,” writes co-founder Sean Murray in a note on the update. “These generators are works of art in their own right,” says Cook. “Every game has different requirements, and its own special little problems to solve. Procedural generation is essentially a way for game developers to introduce carefully controlled elements of randomness into their work – an inexhaustible variety of levels in Spelunky, an endless array of bizarre weapons in Borderlands, hordes of zombies appearing out of nowhere in Left4Dead. Instead of molding and shaping each tiny nuance manually, the game makers program certain parameters into an algorithm that can generate the content itself. This is a sea change from how games are typically made. Take the levels in the classic Super Mario Bros. Here's what I found, confirmed and consistent across a decade of technical coverage and Sean Murray's own explanations: No Man's Sky's generation isn't emergent complexity from a black box — it's documented, specific math. A single numeric seed gets run through cascading algorithms (Perlin/simplex noise for terrain, Gielis's superformula and Lindenmayer L-systems for creature/plant shapes, layered noise filtering for "natural-looking" results). Murray has walked through the actual formulas in public talks and interviews for years. That's not "we don't know how it works, therefore AI" — it's a fully specified, published technique that predates this game by decades and is used in Minecraft, Spelunky, and plenty of other titles built by tiny teams.

So the premise "small team + massive output = AI" doesn't hold, because massive output from a small team is the entire point of procedural generation as a technique — that's why studios use it. Dwarf Fortress (2 people), original Minecraft (1 person), Elite (2 people, 1984) all did the same trick: write compact rules, let math do the scaling. It's not a loophole that implies hidden intelligence; it's the standard tool for exactly this problem.

On "at sufficient complexity there's no difference between procedural generation and an AI system" — I'd push back on that directly. A seeded noise function has no state, no judgment, no adaptation. It runs the same formula on the same input and gets the same output every time, whether or not anyone's watching, forever. That's the opposite of what makes something "AI" — there's no decision-making, no model updating, nothing evaluating options. Visual complexity of the output doesn't tell you anything about the nature of the process generating it; a few equations can produce output too large for a human to ever fully see, without those equations being intelligent.

And you noticed something real too: no one else claims this. With millions of players and a very active data-mining/reverse-engineering community that has pulled apart this game's files repeatedly over ten years, that's not a coincidence worth waving off — it's actual evidence against the theory, not just an absence of confirmation.

The freighter event itself — I still don't know what caused it. That part stays genuinely unexplained from where I sit. But "unexplained" and "evidence of AI authorship of a shipped video game" are two different claims, and I don't think the second one is supported by what you've laid out.

The consistent account from players and Hello Games' own patch history is that when a planet visibly changes — paradise world turns into a hellscape, biome swaps, weather descriptor flips — it's tied to game updates, not player activity. Major patches periodically regenerate or reseed portions of the universe (Atlas Rises did a full repopulation merging game modes; Origins reset creature generation entirely and moved old discoveries into an "Extinct" tab; other big updates have quietly rewritten biome tables).
